meta.audience: The people of Anti-Nephi-Lehi and the Nephites of Zarahemla
meta.location: The land of Nephi, the wilderness, Zarahemla, Jershon
meta.unit: The sons of Mosiah among the Lamanites (Alma 17–26)

world_behind.title: The second slaughter has no war behind it
world_behind.text: Verse 2 says the Amalekites, unable to reach the Nephites, turned on the converts again. The killing in this chapter is displaced anger with nothing left to aim at.

world_behind.title: The converts do not defend themselves twice
world_behind.text: Verse 3 says they again refused arms and again let themselves be killed. Alma 24 established the covenant; this chapter shows it holding under a second test.

world_behind.title: The king expects the Nephites to kill them
world_behind.text: Verse 6 has him name the reason plainly: many murders and sins committed against those people. His fear is a correct assessment of what he deserves.

world_behind.title: He offers slavery and Ammon refuses it
world_behind.text: Verses 8 and 9 have the king propose that his nation serve as slaves until the debt is repaid, and Ammon answer that Nephite law forbids it. Mosiah 2 has Benjamin saying the same thing about his own reign.

world_behind.title: Ammon inquires before he moves
world_behind.text: Verse 7 offers the test and verse 11 carries it out. The exodus of a whole nation waits on a question actually asked.

world_behind.title: The admission goes to a vote
world_behind.text: Verse 21 has the chief judge send a proclamation asking for the voice of the people. A national immigration decision is put to the assembly, and verse 22 is its answer.

world_behind.title: The terms are stated in the same breath as the welcome
world_behind.text: Verse 24 grants Jershon and armies to guard it, on condition that the newcomers fund those armies out of their substance. Generosity and a bill arrive together.

words.text: To make restitution, to pay back what was destroyed. The record uses the word four times and the King James Bible fourteen, where it almost always means fixing the temple. The king proposes to repair many murders by giving his nation into service.

One who seeks. The noun occurs once in scripture. Mormon uses it to name who gets the kind of joy that put Ammon on the ground: the truly penitent and humble seeker of happiness, which makes the joy a consequence of a search rather than an accident.

The land granted to the converts, on the east by the sea and south of Bountiful. It appears twenty-six times, all in Alma. The record never translates the name, and the land becomes the front line of the war in Alma 43.

Property, what a person owns. The record uses the word twenty-seven times, most often in Mosiah 4 and Alma 1 about giving to the poor. Here it names the tax that pays for the army protecting the people who will not fight.

Loathing, revulsion. The word appears twice in this record and never in the King James Bible; the other use is Alma 13, of sin itself. Here the people of Ammon look on shedding blood the way Alma 13 looks on wickedness.

A curved sword. It occurs three times in this record, in Enos, here, and in Alma 44, and never in the King James Bible. Mormon names it beside the sword to say the refusal covered every weapon they had.

phrases.term: They were treated as though they were angels sent from God
phrases.text: Mormon explains why Ammon and his brethren could not stand to watch. The converts loved them and had received them as messengers. The compassion in the verse runs on a relationship built over fourteen years.

phrases.term: The Nephites will destroy us, because of the many murders and sins we have committed
phrases.text: The king's objection to the rescue plan. He is not arguing that the charge is false. He assumes the people he wronged will act on it, and Ammon has to test the assumption before anyone moves.

phrases.term: We will be their slaves until we repair unto them
phrases.text: The king's opening offer for asylum. He proposes to hand over the liberty of a nation as compensation, which is the measure of how he weighs what they did.

phrases.term: It is against the law of our brethren... that there should be any slaves among them
phrases.text: Ammon refuses the offer on legal grounds. A Nephite prince tells a Lamanite king that his own country will not take what is being offered, and redirects him to rely on mercy instead.

phrases.term: Satan has great hold on the hearts of the Amalekites
phrases.text: The Lord's own reading of the situation, given as the reason to leave. The instruction is to get out, and the assessment of the enemy comes attached to it rather than a promise of protection in place.

phrases.term: We will try the hearts of our brethren
phrases.text: Ammon leaves an entire nation camped in the wilderness while he goes to find out whether they are welcome. The test is of Nephite hearts, and the record uses the same verb it uses for assaying metal.

phrases.term: Joy which none receiveth save it be the truly penitent and humble seeker of happiness
phrases.text: Mormon interrupts the narrative to say who this kind of joy is for. The qualification matches Alma 26, where the penitent are the ones who can know. Joy and knowledge are put behind the same door.

phrases.term: Their joy was not that to exceed their strength
phrases.text: Mormon notes that Alma, Aaron, Omner, and Himni stayed on their feet. The observation is almost dry, and it makes Ammon's collapse a fact about Ammon instead of a general rule.

phrases.term: Desiring the voice of the people concerning the admitting their brethren
phrases.text: The chief judge puts a question of national admission to a vote. The reign of the judges is nine chapters old, and this is what Mosiah's reform looks like operating on something difficult.

phrases.term: On condition that they will give us a portion of their substance
phrases.text: The Nephites attach a price to the protection. They will guard a people who will not fight, and the people who will not fight will pay for the guarding. The record puts the arrangement on paper without comment.

phrases.term: Death was swallowed up to them by the victory of Christ over it
phrases.text: Paul's sentence from 1 Corinthians 15:54, applied to a nation that has decided to be killed rather than kill. Mormon gives the doctrine as the reason they could hold the covenant.

verses.label: v. 6–10
verses.title: A refugee negotiation stopped by a statute
verses.text: The record sets down an exchange whose sticking point is law, not fear. The king offers the only terms he thinks are available: "we will be their slaves until we repair unto them the many murders and sins which we have committed against them." Ammon refuses on a legal ground and names its author: "It is against the law of our brethren, which was established by my father, that there should be any slaves among them." The obstacle to a people saving their lives is a Nephite prohibition on slavery, and the record states it as a settled rule instead of an argument.

verses.label: v. 7–13
verses.title: Four steps of a consultation, all of them recorded
verses.text: The record keeps the whole procedure and not merely its result. Ammon proposes a conditional in advance: "I will go and inquire of the Lord, and if he say unto us, go down unto our brethren, will ye go?" The king agrees to be bound by the answer before hearing it, twice, at verses 8 and 10. The inquiry follows at verse 11, the answer stands whole at verse 12, and verse 13 reports it being carried back. Nothing is skipped, including the agreement to obey an answer nobody has yet.

verses.label: v. 12
verses.title: The reason given for leaving is a political one
verses.text: The instruction attributed to the Lord makes no appeal to righteousness or promise: "Get this people out of this land, that they perish not; for Satan has great hold on the hearts of the Amalekites, who do stir up the Lamanites to anger against their brethren to slay them." The cause of the danger is located in one named faction and its influence over another, and the remedy is relocation. It reads as a threat assessment, and the record gives it in full.

verses.label: v. 17–19
verses.title: A question the record asks about its own scene
verses.text: After describing Ammon's joy as strength failing him and falling to the earth, the record stops and puts a question to the reader: "Now was not this exceeding joy? Behold, this is joy which none receiveth save it be the truly penitent and humble seeker of happiness." Then verse 19 makes a comparison and declines to rank it: the joy of Alma and the others was great, "but behold their joy was not that to exceed their joy." Brethren stands twenty-five times in this chapter, more than in any chapter of the Bible or this volume.

verses.label: v. 21–24
verses.title: Immigration decided by referendum, with terms
verses.text: The chief judge does not rule. He "sent a proclamation throughout all the land, desiring the voice of the people concerning the admitting their brethren." The answer is quoted in the first person plural and contains three items: a named territory with its boundaries, "the land of Jershon, which is on the east by the sea"; a military commitment, "we will set our armies between the land Jershon and the land Nephi"; and a price, "on condition that they will give us a portion of their substance to assist us that we may maintain our armies." Verse 23 even supplies the reason the refugees cannot defend themselves, so the terms are set out with the case for them.

verses.label: v. 26
verses.title: A new name, and who gave it
verses.text: The record notes the naming and attributes it: "they were called by the Nephites the people of Ammon; therefore they were distinguished by that name ever after." The people who took the name Anti-Nephi-Lehi for themselves in Alma 24:3 are given a second name by their hosts, this one after a foreign missionary. The record uses the new one from here forward and does not say whether they chose it.

verses.label: v. 28–30
verses.title: A description built out of what they will not do
verses.text: The closing characterisation is stated almost entirely in negatives: "they did look upon shedding the blood of their brethren with the greatest abhorrence; and they never could be prevailed upon to take up arms against their brethren." Verse 29 pushes it to the limit, "they would suffer death in the most aggravating and distressing manner which could be inflicted by their brethren, before they would take the sword." Only in verse 30 does the record turn positive, and it does so in four words: "a zealous and beloved people."

chapter.title: The covenant is tested a second time and holds
chapter.text: Alma 24 could be read as a single decision under pressure. Alma 27 shows the same people making it again, with the outcome already known, and Mormon records both refusals.

chapter.title: The rescue is proposed by the people who converted them
chapter.text: Verse 4 supplies the reason in the missionaries' own terms, that they were "treated as though they were angels sent from God to save them from everlasting destruction," and verse 5 gives the proposal as a plan of movement, "let us go down to the land of Zarahemla... and flee out of the hands of our enemies." Verse 3 has stated the alternative and its cost, that the people "suffered themselves to be slain according to the desires of their enemies." A mission that began at Alma 17:6 ends in evacuation logistics.

chapter.title: The king's guilt is accurate and it still does not decide the case
chapter.text: He is right about what his people did. Ammon takes the fear seriously enough to inquire, and the answer is to go anyway and rely on mercy.

chapter.title: Slavery is refused by the country being offered it
chapter.text: The king offers at verse 8, "we will be their slaves until we repair unto them the many murders and sins which we have committed." The refusal at verse 9 cites a statute and names its author: "It is against the law of our brethren, which was established by my father, that there should be any slaves among them." Mosiah 2:13 has Benjamin state the same policy of his own reign, "neither have I suffered that ye should be confined in dungeons, nor that ye should make slaves one of another." An offer of national servitude is declined on legal grounds.

chapter.title: A vote decides a nation's border
chapter.text: The chief judge asks and the people answer. Mosiah 29 argued that the voice of the people usually chooses right, and this chapter is the case where it does.

chapter.title: The welcome comes with an invoice
chapter.text: Verses 22 through 24 set out three terms in order: the land of Jershon, located by three boundaries; armies stationed "between the land Jershon and the land Nephi"; and a payment, "on condition that they will give us a portion of their substance to assist us that we may maintain our armies." Verse 23 states the reason for the arrangement in the Nephites' own words, "on account of their fear to take up arms against their brethren lest they should commit sin." Alma 43:13 later reports the levy being paid. A defense paid for by people who will not fight is entered as a condition of the grant.

chapter.title: Joy is treated as a physical event
chapter.text: Ammon is swallowed up to the exhausting of his strength, and Mormon carefully notes that the other three were not. Alma 19 and Alma 22 had kings on the floor for the same reason.

chapter.title: They get a third name
chapter.text: Lamanites, then Anti-Nephi-Lehies, then the people of Ammon, given by Nephites and kept ever after. Each renaming marks a change in who they are attached to.

applications.title: Ask before you assume the answer
applications.text: The king was sure the Nephites would destroy them; Ammon's reply is not reassurance but a proposal to find out, "I will go and inquire of the Lord, and if he say unto us, go down unto our brethren, will ye go?" Settle the question rather than the mood.

applications.title: Refuse the payment someone offers out of guilt
applications.text: The king offers national slavery as restitution, "we will be their slaves until we repair unto them the many murders." Ammon refuses on legal grounds, "It is against the law of our brethren." When somebody tries to buy back a wrong at a price you should not take, name the rule rather than the sentiment.

applications.title: Rely on mercy where you cannot make restitution
applications.text: The alternative Ammon proposes is uncomfortable, "let us go down and rely upon the mercies of our brethren." Some debts cannot be paid, and the only available move is to stand exposed and ask.

applications.title: Put the hard question to the whole group
applications.text: The chief judge does not decide, he publishes: a proclamation "desiring the voice of the people concerning the admitting their brethren." A decision that will cost everybody is one everybody should be asked about.

applications.title: State the conditions with the offer
applications.text: The Nephites promise land and armies and then say what they want for it, "on condition that they will give us a portion of their substance to assist us." An offer with its terms attached is honest in a way that generosity followed by an invoice is not.

applications.title: Say why you are doing it
applications.text: The reason is written into the grant, "on account of their fear to take up arms against their brethren lest they should commit sin." Explaining a concession is what stops it being resented later by the people making it.

applications.title: Tell your own story when you ask others to change theirs
applications.text: Alma comes back with Ammon and "related unto them his conversion." A man asking a nation to uproot itself first said what had happened to him.

applications.title: Let the new name come from the people who took them in
applications.text: They were "called by the Nephites the people of Ammon; therefore they were distinguished by that name ever after." Names given by hosts are worth noticing; this one records who they were received by rather than what they had been.

questions.text: What have I decided once that I would have to decide again if it were tested?
What am I sure I would be condemned for, and have I ever checked?
What am I overpaying for something I have already been forgiven?
Whose heart have I refused to try because I was afraid of the answer?
When did I last feel joy I would call too big for me?
What have I agreed to help with while leaving the cost unsaid?
What would change if I stopped looking at death with any degree of terror?
